passage:
"Raghav, stay back a minute?" Jeevan, the geography teacher, said as the others ran out.
Raghav froze by the door. "Did I do something?"
"No. I read your answer on why the river changes course. Two pages. Nobody else thought about the farmers."
Raghav looked at his shoes. "I knew it in class. The words just get stuck when everyone turns round."
"That's all right. You haven't raised your hand once this term, and I'd started to wonder if geography bored you."
"It's my favourite."
"Then here's a deal. Every Friday, write me one question or idea on a slip. I'll read the good ones out, without your name if you like."
"With my name," Raghav said quietly. "Maybe."

qa.q: What did Raghav's answer think about that nobody else did?
qa.a: Raghav thought about the farmers; nobody else did.

qa.q: What had Jeevan been feeling about Raghav's silence in class before reading the answer?
qa.a: Jeevan had been a little worried, starting to wonder if geography bored Raghav, until the two-page answer showed how much Raghav cared.

qa.q: What choice did Jeevan make once Raghav explained that the words get stuck?
qa.a: Jeevan offered a Friday slip for written questions and ideas, a route that does not need a raised hand.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel about geography class once the Friday slips begin?
qa.a: He may feel seen and less pressured, able to show what he knows without everyone turning round.

grounding: A teacher realises a silent boy's written answer shows deep interest and offers him a written way to take part.

passage:
In my first year teaching Class 4, I nearly wrote "lacks interest" on Vandana's report. She never raised her hand. When I asked her something in front of the class, she went pink and whispered, "I don't know." Then I marked the story-writing test. Hers was about a lighthouse keeper's daughter who counted ships, and it made me put my pen down. After school, just the two of us, I asked her what happened to the ships. She talked for ten minutes. After that I started a question box and let children answer some questions in their notebooks instead of aloud. Vandana's notebook filled up. I crossed out that line on the report before anyone saw it.
Jaya

qa.a: A lighthouse keeper's daughter who counted ships.

qa.q: What does Vandana going pink and whispering "I don't know" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt anxious being put on the spot aloud, not that she didn't know or care.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Jaya ran the class?
qa.a: Reading Vandana's story and talking with her alone led Jaya to start a question box and notebook answers.

qa.q: What would have changed for Vandana if "lacks interest" had stayed on the report?
qa.a: Her family and next teacher might have seen her as uninterested, and her thoughtful side could have stayed hidden.

grounding: A teacher looks back on nearly mistaking a silent girl for an uninterested one, and on offering written and one-to-one ways to answer.
